fixes.explanation: Right, baker. "The fierce anger of the LORD will not turn back until He has fully accomplished the purposes of His heart." (Jeremiah 30:24) So the statement had it backward, because the anger does not turn back before the job is done. The verse ends with this: "In the days to come you will understand this."

I can see why you'd go there, but the LORD says nothing about the temple here. He tells Jeremiah, "Write in a book all the words that I have spoken to you." (Jeremiah 30:2) The job is writing, and it covers every word He has spoken.

Not quite, friend. The LORD doesn't tell Jeremiah to keep anything to himself. He says, "Write in a book all the words that I have spoken to you." (Jeremiah 30:2) The instruction is to write them in a book.

I get why it might feel that way, friend. But the LORD says, "…I will restore from captivity My people Israel and Judah…" (Jeremiah 30:3) Nothing in that promise says He leaves them there for good. He says He will restore them to the land that He gave to their fathers.

A visit is a nice little trip, friend, but that's not the word the LORD uses. He says He will restore them to the land that He gave to their fathers, "…and they will possess it." (Jeremiah 30:3) Possess is a much bigger word than visit.

Red is what happens when you're embarrassed or mad, and that's not the picture here. The LORD says He sees "…every face turned pale?" (Jeremiah 30:6) In this kind of terror the color runs out of the face instead of rushing in. Think of the drop in your stomach when flashing lights show up in your rearview mirror.

I can see why you'd pick it, friend, but that's not what the LORD says. He promises, "…no longer will strangers enslave them." (Jeremiah 30:8) Then comes the turn: "Instead, they will serve the LORD their God and David their king…" (Jeremiah 30:9) The word "instead" does all the work.

Here's what the verse says, friend. The LORD says, "As for you, O Jacob My servant, do not be afraid, declares the LORD…" and then, "For I will surely save you out of a distant place…" (Jeremiah 30:10) He names Jacob as His servant and promises to save him from far away. So this one is true.

Hard labor is not what the LORD promises, friend. He says, "Jacob will return to quiet and ease, with no one to make him afraid." (Jeremiah 30:10) The promise is quiet and ease. Nobody is making him afraid.

That's it. The LORD says, "All your lovers have forgotten you; they no longer seek you…" (Jeremiah 30:14) Nobody pleads their cause, and the lovers no longer seek them. I think that's a lonely spot, friend.

Nobody's reaching for a wallet here. The LORD says, "All your lovers have forgotten you; they no longer seek you…" (Jeremiah 30:14) The verse says nothing about anyone paying. The verse before says there's no one to plead their cause (Jeremiah 30:13).

That's not the reason the LORD gives, friend. He says, "…they call you an outcast, Zion, for whom no one cares." (Jeremiah 30:17) The verse doesn't mention anyone asking Him. His reason is what they call her.

That one's not in the verse, friend. The LORD said her pain has no cure (Jeremiah 30:15). His reason for healing is "…because they call you an outcast, Zion, for whom no one cares." (Jeremiah 30:17) And He is the one who says, "…I will restore your health and heal your wounds…"

I get why you'd think so, friend. But the LORD says, "Thanksgiving will proceed from them, a sound of celebration." (Jeremiah 30:19) The sound He names is celebration, not weeping. Thanksgiving is what's coming.

Babylon isn't the answer the verse gives, friend. The LORD says, "Their leader will be one of their own, and their ruler will arise from their midst." (Jeremiah 30:21) The verse says where he comes from, and it's their midst. He rises up among them.

That's it, baker. "Behold, the storm of the LORD has gone out with fury, a whirlwind swirling down upon the heads of the wicked." (Jeremiah 30:23) The verse names who the whirlwind falls on. I think this is a heavy verse, and it's worth reading slowly.
The verse doesn't name the prophets, friend. It says the whirlwind comes "…swirling down upon the heads of the wicked." (Jeremiah 30:23) The wicked are the ones the text names.

Good guess, since the exiles come up a lot in this passage. But the verse says the whirlwind comes "…swirling down upon the heads of the wicked." (Jeremiah 30:23) Earlier, the LORD promises to restore His people from captivity (Jeremiah 30:3), and this verse names the wicked.
